arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Laycock argued forty prison systems allow beards. He stated Arkansas rejects evidence to seek absolute deference.
Curran argued the beard aids disguise. He claimed it threatens identification and contraband concealment.
Yang argued the state failed its burden. He stated forty states allow such beards without issue.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Salah Horn argues his faith requires a beard. Arkansas officials ban beards to prevent contraband and disguise. The lower court sided with the state. Horn asks the Supreme Court to reverse that result.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on October 7, 2014.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Horn wants the Court to strike down the beard ban. He argues his religious rights outweigh the state's security claims.
Arkansas wants the Court to uphold the beard ban. It argues the rule is essential for maximum security.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Horn's counsel argues forty other prison systems allow beards. They claim Arkansas rejects valid evidence to gain absolute deference.
Arkansas's counsel argues a half-inch beard aids disguise. They claim this threatens identification and contraband concealment.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked if a quarter-inch rule would satisfy the standard. She noted other inmates receive similar accommodations.
Justice Kennedy asked if RLUIPA displaces the Turner standard. He questioned the specific burden on prisons under strict scrutiny.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the balance between religious freedom and prison security. It sets the standard for evaluating inmate accommodation requests. The outcome impacts how states manage religious practices in custody.
